root_idea.summary: The root centers on the shighāf, the covering or inner part of the heart, and conveys penetration to the heart’s interior and intense emotional attachment.
root_idea.development: From the anatomical heart covering, the root develops the sense of love reaching or striking the heart’s interior, then extends to deep attachment, vehement fondness, and figurative disturbance of the mind.

qac_form_accounting.reason: The canonical Quran-attested Form I verb is presented under its normalized perfect citation form.

senses.definition: To penetrate to the shighāf of the heart with love, thereby deeply affecting, impassioning, or taking hold of someone.
senses.usage_conditions: In the Quranic construction, love is described as reaching, striking, or passing beneath the heart’s inner covering. The related noun شَغَفٌ denotes love that reaches the shighāf; the underlying anatomical term may be understood as the heart’s covering or inner part.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To strike or smite the shighāf, the heart’s covering or inner part.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A literal bodily use, compared with striking the liver; the Quranic love construction is the figurative emotional development of this action.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To become attached to or love someone; to be vehemently fond of or desirous of something.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The forms and constructions vary in vocalization and voice, while expressing the same branch of intense attachment or fondness.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of property: to become embellished or pleasing to someone, so that the person loves it.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A construction in which property is the subject and its pleasing appearance produces attachment in the person concerned.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To become disquieted or disturbed by something.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A distinct emotional result from the construction expressing fondness or desire.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Figuratively, to put vain suggestions into people’s minds and separate them.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Reported of a saying or judicial sentence in an expression comparing its effect to entering the shighāf of people’s hearts.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The bark or outer layer of the ghāf tree.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A homonymous botanical noun, distinct from the emotional and anatomical branches.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The pericardium or covering of the heart; by extension or variant, an inner part, core, or fatty layer of the heart.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Classical authorities also identify it with the heart’s membrane, a place associated with the entry of phlegm, or in one report the heart itself; these are variant anatomical identifications.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A disease or pain beneath the ribs or in the right side, including abdominal pain or a disease affecting the heart’s shighāf.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: One reported description says that the disease is fatal if it reaches the spleen.
An adjectival use recorded alongside the sense of being intensely attached or enamored.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Deeply enamored of property because it has been made pleasing or attractive to the person.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A passive-participial construction describing intense fondness for wealth or property.

lane_unit_coverage.note: Covers the literal heart-covering action, the Quranic love construction, attachment, fondness, property becoming pleasing, and disturbance.
The noun شَغَفٌ is the love-reaching-the-heart branch subsumed under the Quranic sense.
Anatomical meanings and their reported variant identifications.
Disease and pain meanings associated with شَغَافٌ.
Pointer-only reference to the preceding شَغَافٌ entry.
The adjective’s madness and intense-fondness uses.

cautions: The verb has one supplied Quranic occurrence, in 12:30; its contextual translation as “impassioned” reflects the image of love reaching the heart’s inner covering.
Classical descriptions of the shighāf’s precise anatomy vary, including the heart’s covering, inner core, fatty layer, and related structures.
